dicas.texto: Boa pergunta! Quando representamos uma fração na reta numérica, em quantas partes devemos dividir cada unidade? Pense: o denominador nos diz isso!
Você está no caminho certo! Divida o trecho de 0 a 1 em 7 partes iguais, depois faça o mesmo de 1 a 2. Depois conte 8 dessas partes a partir do zero.
Quase lá! Como o denominador é 7, cada parte representa 1/7. Conte 8 dessas partes começando do zero — onde você para?
Você está muito perto! Marque o ponto após passar 1 inteiro e mais 1/7. Isso é exatamente 8/7!
Ótima observação! O que acontece quando o numerador e o denominador são iguais? Que número isso representa?
Continue assim! Divida o trecho de 0 a 1 em 8 partes iguais. Depois, conte 8 partes a partir do zero — onde isso te leva?
Quase lá! Se cada parte é 1/8, então 8 partes juntas formam exatamente... quanto? Olhe para o final do primeiro segmento da reta!
Você está quase concluindo! Conte: 1/8, 2/8, ..., até 8/8. Isso termina exatamente no número 1. Marque esse ponto!

dicas.texto: Which two fractional amounts of time appear in the story?
Read the numerator and denominator together for each runner before comparing the amounts.
Christin's time is written with 8 on top and 7 on the bottom.
Select the fraction that has numerator 8 and denominator 7 for Christin's running time.
What does the denominator tell us about the equal parts on a number line?
Look at the bottom number in Christin's fraction and enter that number in the denominator field.
In 8/7, the bottom number is 7, not 8.
Type 7 in the denom1 field and confirm it to create seven equal parts.
How many sevenths do you need to count from zero?
Count one equal interval for each numerator unit, starting with 1/7 at the first mark.
Seven sevenths reaches 1, so the next seventh is just to the right of 1.
Click the eighth seventh mark, immediately to the right of the point labeled 1.
What does the denominator tell us about the partitions on Trisha's number line?
Read the bottom number of Trisha's fraction and enter it in the second denominator field.
Trisha's fraction is 8/8, so its denominator is 8.
Type 8 in the denom2 field and confirm it to create eight equal parts.
What happens when the numerator and denominator are the same?
Count all eight equal eighths from zero until you reach the whole-number mark.
The eighth mark is the point labeled 1, because eight eighths make one whole.
Click the point at 1, which is the eighth mark on the number line.
On a number line, which point represents the greater amount?
Compare the horizontal positions of the two marked points rather than comparing only their numerators.
Trisha's point is at 1, while Christin's point is slightly to the right of 1.
Choose the runner whose marked point is farther to the right on the number lines.
Which runner's point is farther from zero on the number lines?
Use the order of the marked points to choose the matching comparison statement.
Christin's 8/7 is beyond 1, while Trisha's 8/8 is exactly 1.
Select the option stating that the runner with the point to the right ran more hours.
What does a fraction greater than 1 lo... like on a number line?
Check that the first marked point is beyond 1 and the second marked point is exactly at 1.
Christin's fraction has one more seventh than the seven sevenths needed to make 1.
After confirming the two points and the comparison choice, press Done to finish the exercise.

exercicio.statement:
A local charity set up a running event for fund raising and a bunch of kids signed up to help. The longer the amount of time they run, the more money their sponsors will donate.
Christin ran for 8/7 hours.
Trisha ran for 8/8 hours
Who ran for more hours?

steps.instruction: Use the fraction models to identify the two running times that must be compared.

Set Trisha's number line to 8 equal parts between each whole number.
Compare the marked points on the two number lines.
Select the statement that correctly compares their running times.
Confirm the completed comparison by pressing Done.
